U5 Fixed (static) partitioning

 Definition
 The number of non-overlapping partitions in RAM is fixed and made before execution (at system configuration); sizes may or may not be equal. No spanning — a
 process must fit entirely in one partition. Each partition holds at most one process, so degree of multiprogramming = number of partitions.




 Advantages Disadvantages
 • Easy to implement — put a process in a suitable partition • Internal fragmentation — a small program still takes a whole partition
 • Little OS overhead • External fragmentation — scattered free partitions can’t be combined
 • A process larger than the largest partition cannot run
 • Limits the degree of multiprogramming




 Example — partitions 4, 8, 8, 16 MB (Partioining in OS.docx)
 P1 = 1, P2 = 7, P3 = 7, P4 = 14 MB. Internal fragmentation = (4−1)+(8−7)+(8−7)+(16−14) = 3+1+1+2 = 7 MB. A new 7 MB process P5 cannot load although 7 MB is free in
 total (spread over four partitions) → external fragmentation. A 32 MB process is invalid.

U5 Variable (dynamic) partitioning

 Definition
 Partitions are not made in advance. RAM starts empty and a partition equal to the process size is created at run time → no internal fragmentation, no limit on
 process size (except total RAM), no fixed limit on multiprogramming. Memory then contains holes. When a process exits its partition is freed and adjacent free
 partitions are combined. The OS keeps a table of allocated partitions and free partitions (holes).




 Advantages Disadvantages
 • No internal fragmentation • External fragmentation (holes appear as processes come and go)
 • No restriction on degree of multiprogramming • Harder to implement — allocation at run time
 • No limit on process size • Needs compaction or a good placement algorithm
